column1: Reconstruct Argument 1: The true is the whole: against beginning from the immediate (PhG Preface).
column2:
Aim: philosophy cannot start from a first principle, an immediate certainty or an intuition of the Absolute and derive the rest; the truth of a claim is the whole development that reaches it, so a science of knowledge must begin from the poorest standpoint consciousness has and earn every step.
Premises: the stages of a development are "moments of an organic unity" (PhG ¶2); a starting point stated immediately is merely the universal: "If we say 'all animals,' that does not pass for zoology" (PhG ¶20); so a first principle, "even if it is true, is yet none the less false just because and in so far as it is merely a fundamental proposition, merely a first principle" (PhG ¶24); an Absolute in which all differences vanish is "the night in which, as we say, all cows are black" (PhG ¶16); Kant's testing of knowledge before using it already assumes the split in question, and we should "take care lest the fear of error is not just the initial error" (PhG ¶74).
Conclusion: "The truth is the whole" (PhG ¶20); the Absolute is "essentially a result" (PhG ¶20), and sense-consciousness must undertake "a long and laborious journey" (PhG ¶27), the Phenomenology.
Objection: philosophy is left with no place to stand: every claim on the way is provisional, and the beginning is arbitrary or borrowed from the end (Schelling's Munich and Berlin lectures). Kierkegaard: no existing person stands at the end of the system. Feuerbach (1839): the presuppositionless start is staged.
Reply: Hegel accepts a circle and denies it is vicious: true reality is "the circle which presupposes its end or its purpose, and has its end for its beginning" (PhG ¶18); the beginning is the reader's own standpoint, tested by its own standard (PhG ¶84); provisional is not false. Open: metaphysical holism (Beiser; Houlgate, Stern) or the space of justification (Pippin, Pinkard); Houlgate against Pippin on a presuppositionless beginning.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 2: Substance as subject (PhG Preface ¶¶17–25).
column2:
Aim: what is ultimately real must be grasped not only as substance, a being that simply is what it is, but also as subject, an activity that differentiates itself, relates to itself in its differences and knows itself; its name is spirit.
Premises: in Spinoza's One Substance "self-consciousness was simply submerged, and not preserved" (PhG ¶17); merely subjective thinking, or an immediate identity of thought and being, falls "back into that inert, abstract simplicity" (PhG ¶17); "The living substance, further, is that being which is truly subject", and "As subject it is pure and simple negativity" (PhG ¶18); a unity that never goes through difference is insipid "if it lacks the seriousness, the suffering, the patience, and the labour of the negative" (PhG ¶19); as Aristotle saw, "reason is purposive activity" (PhG ¶22); an ordinary proposition cannot show this, since in it "The subject is taken to be a fixed point" (PhG ¶23).
Conclusion: "that substance is essentially subject, is expressed in the idea which represents the Absolute as Spirit (Geist)" (PhG ¶25); "Spirit is the only Reality" (PhG ¶25).
Objection: Feuerbach, Provisional Theses (1842): Hegel inverts subject and predicate; the real subjects are finite human beings and nature, thought is their predicate, so the thesis is theology in logical dress (Marx applied the inversion to the Philosophy of Right in 1843). Analytic form: a self-positing substance is either mysticism or an unexplained metaphor (Russell).
Reply (the literature's, in two competing forms): metaphysical: reality is a self-developing whole that knows itself in and through finite knowers, not a cosmic person (Beiser's organic monism; Houlgate, Stern; Taylor's cosmic subject). Post-Kantian: subject means a self-determining activity whose norms a community institutes and revises (Pippin, Pinkard, Brandom). Open: this is the main division in the field; how much is theology (Taylor, Beiser against Kojève's atheist reading).

column1: Reconstruct Argument 3: Sense-certainty refutes itself (PhG ¶¶90–110).
column2:
Aim: the claim to know a bare particular, a this, immediately and without concepts, fails on its own terms; whatever sense-certainty can say or point to is a universal, so even the most immediate knowledge is mediated.
Premises: sense-certainty takes itself to be "knowledge of the immediate, of what is" (PhG ¶90); asked "What is the Now?" it answers "the Now is night-time", but if we write it down, since "A truth cannot lose anything by being written down", by noon "it has turned stale and become out of date" (PhG ¶95); what survives is "not something immediate but something mediated" (PhG ¶96), and the Here likewise; in saying this we utter a universal: "Language, however, as we see, is the more truthful" (PhG ¶97); placing the truth in the I fails too, since "I is merely universal" (PhG ¶102); pointing is itself a process of many Nows and Heres (PhG ¶¶107–108).
Conclusion: "universality is the real truth of sense-certainty" (PhG ¶97); what it hoped to grasp outside language is "something barely and simply 'meant'" (PhG ¶110). It passes to perception, the thing with properties.
Objection: Feuerbach (1839): Hegel refutes the word this, not the thing; sensuous being is real for a sensuous being who sees and eats, and Hegel's jibe at animals that "fall-to without more ado and eat them up" (PhG ¶109) concedes it. Philosophy of language: an indexical sentence expresses a new proposition on each use, so the noon test changes the claim.
Reply (the literature's): sense-certainty claimed to know particulars fully, not merely that they exist, and both objections give that up. Fixing what now it is night says needs a rule from contexts to times and an order of earlier and later: the universal and mediation Hegel names. Singular reference depends on general concepts (SEP's reading). Open: transcendental argument (Taylor), theory of concepts (Pippin, Brandom) or ontology (Houlgate); McDowell's Sellarsian reading against Westphal's realism.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 4: Perception: the thing and its many properties (PhG ¶¶111–131).
column2:
Aim: the commonsense thing, one unit with many independent properties, cannot be held together on its own terms, since its unity and its properties keep displacing one another; a thing is what it is only through its relations to others, which points on to forces and laws.
Premises: the object is a one and an also: "This salt is a simple Here and at the same time manifold: it is white, and also pungent, also cubical in shape, also of a specific weight, and so on" (PhG ¶113); its standard is the object's self-identity, so any conflict is laid to consciousness, which learns "the possibility of deception" (PhG ¶116); first strategy, the diversity is ours: the thing is "merely white to our eyes, also sharp to our tongue" (PhG ¶119), but each property is determinate only by opposition, and through its properties the thing excludes others (PhG ¶120); second strategy, the unity is ours, yet "so far as it is white it is not cubical" (PhG ¶121); third strategy, one in itself and many for others, or essential and inessential properties, yet the inessential are necessary, "a distinction that only exists in words" (PhG ¶127).
Conclusion: the thing's unity and its being for others cannot be kept apart; common sense, which "is always poorest where it pretends to be richest" (PhG ¶131), cannot save it. The sensible this was superseded, and "to supersede (aufheben) is at once to negate and to preserve" (PhG ¶113).
Objection: Russell: Hegel confuses the is of predication with the is of identity; a logic of predicates and relations dissolves the contradiction, and the new logic overturned Hegel's metaphysics. Second: the contradictions are tensions in particular theories of the thing, which a better theory avoids.
Reply (the literature's): Hegel does not deny that one subject has many predicates; he asks what makes them properties of one thing, which formal logic takes for granted. Stern (1990): neither bundle nor substratum explains the unity; Hegel's answer is a substance-kind. Better theories escape only by doing what the next chapter does. Debt: the verdict on in so far as clauses is quick. Open: metaphysics of the object (Stern, Houlgate) or a knower's entitlements (Pippin, Pinkard); Harris on Locke and Hume; Brandom's exclusive difference.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 5: Force, the understanding and the inverted world (PhG ¶¶132–165).
column2:
Aim: the understanding, which explains appearances by forces and laws in a world behind them, finds in that inner world only the structure of its own explaining; the split between appearance and a supersensible reality collapses, and consciousness of an object proves to be self-consciousness.
Premises: the thing becomes force, which expresses itself and is solicited by another force (PhG ¶¶135–141); force is never perceived, and the understanding "looks through the intervening play of forces into the real and true background of things" (PhG ¶143); but the inner world has only appearance's content: "The supersensible is then appearance qua appearance" (PhG ¶147), first stable as "a quiescent 'kingdom of laws'" (PhG ¶149); explanation gives the force exactly the law's content, "an explanation that not only explains nothing" (PhG ¶¶154–155); taken as a second world, the inner world "has turned round into its opposite" (PhG ¶157), an inverted world where the sweet is sour and punishment becomes grace (PhG ¶158); it is the first world's own inner difference: "We have to think pure flux, opposition within opposition itself, or Contradiction" (PhG ¶160), which Hegel calls infinity.
Conclusion: in the inner world "understanding merely experiences itself" (PhG ¶165); "behind the so-called curtain, which is to hide the inner world, there is nothing to be seen unless we ourselves go behind there" (PhG ¶165).
Objection: philosophy of science: Newton's law unifies terrestrial and celestial motion and predicts, so explanation is not tautological, and the understanding has found the world, not itself. Popper, What is Dialectic? (1940): accepting contradictions as true would wreck science, since from a contradiction anything follows.
Reply (the literature's): the tautology charge targets hidden powers in a second world; unification is a relation among laws, close to a regularity or structural view. Priest (1989): Popper presupposes non-contradiction, and a paraconsistent logic blocks explosion; others read Hegel's contradiction as a whole made of opposed moments, like a magnet's poles (Wandschneider: only apparent contradiction). Debt: the step to self-consciousness rests on infinity. Open: Gadamer against Pinkard on the inverted world; Pippin against Houlgate on why consciousness becomes self-consciousness.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 6: Self-consciousness is desire, and desire needs another self-consciousness (PhG ¶¶166–177).
column2:
Aim: self-consciousness is not a quiet inner awareness but a practical relation to the world, desire, which assures itself by negating what is other; consuming things can never achieve this, so it can be satisfied only by another self-consciousness, and the self is social from the start.
Premises: self-consciousness is the result of Argument 5, a self that "is essentially the return out of otherness" (PhG ¶167); the world remains, taken as negative, and a self that proves its independence by negating it "is primarily desire" (PhG ¶168); meanwhile "the object has become Life" (PhG ¶168); desire assures itself by consuming its object (PhG ¶174); but "In this state of satisfaction, however, it has experience of the independence of its object", and it "rather produces it again, as well as the desire" (PhG ¶175); so it "can only attain satisfaction when this object itself effectually brings about negation within itself" (PhG ¶175), which only a consciousness can do.
Conclusion: "Self-consciousness attains its satisfaction only in another self-consciousness" (PhG ¶175); "With this we already have before us the notion of Mind or Spirit" (PhG ¶177), "Ego that is 'we,' a plurality of Egos, and 'we' that is a single Ego" (PhG ¶177).
Objection: premise 6 is a non sequitur: endless desire shows only that desire is endless, and a tool or a tame animal also yields to its owner (Neuhouser and Pippin call the step among the most compressed in the book). Marx (1844): Hegel makes the human being self-consciousness, when it is a natural, sensuous being with needs and independent objects.
Reply (the literature's): desire wants proof that it counts, not pleasure; a consumed thing proves nothing, and only a being with its own point of view can acknowledge that the self is the standard, which no tool or animal does. Against Marx: the self is already living and desiring, and the next section makes it a working self. Open: Kojève's desire for another's desire; McDowell's one-self allegory against Pippin's literal sociality; Fichte's summons (SEP); Siep and Honneth on Jena.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 7: The struggle for recognition (PhG ¶¶178–188).
column2:
Aim: a self-consciousness exists as such only in being recognized by another; recognition in its pure concept is mutual; but the first attempt to win it, each proving it is not bound to life, takes the form of a life-and-death struggle, which defeats its own aim if either party dies.
Premises: "Self-consciousness exists in itself and for itself, in that, and by the fact that it exists for another self-consciousness; that is to say, it is only by being acknowledged or 'recognised'" (PhG ¶178); meeting another, it "has come outside itself" (PhG ¶179); "Action from one side only would be useless" (PhG ¶182), and in the pure concept "They recognise themselves as mutually recognising one another" (PhG ¶184); but they first meet as living individuals, and the concept first appears as its opposite, where "one is merely recognised, while the other only recognises" (PhG ¶185); to show it is not tied to life each seeks the other's death and risks its own: "it is solely by risking life, that freedom is obtained" (PhG ¶187).
Conclusion: the struggle is necessary at this stage: "The individual, who has not staked his life, may, no doubt, be recognised as a Person; but he has not attained the truth of this recognition as an independent self-consciousness" (PhG ¶187). Carried to death, it is self-defeating: "Their act is abstract negation" (PhG ¶188). So one party yields.
Objection: the fight is unmotivated: if recognition is reciprocal in concept, give it. Honneth (1992): the Phenomenology narrows the Jena account of love, law and esteem to one confrontation; Benjamin (1988): the first recognition is a parent's care. Hobbes's state of nature with prestige for gain.
Reply (the literature's, with Hegel's text): the struggle is the first, failed attempt of a self that knows nothing yet of mutuality, and Hegel says it defeats itself (PhG ¶188); risking life dramatizes that a free self's commitments can outweigh any natural desire; Hegel is not writing developmental psychology, and love appears in the family as recognition of a member, not an independent agent. Open: history (Kojève) or conceptual reconstruction (Pippin, Pinkard); Brandom on normative authority; Siep and Honneth against Williams on Jena.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 8: Lordship and bondage: the reversal through fear and work (PhG ¶¶189–196).
column2:
Aim: the relation of lord and bondsman defeats the lord's aim, since he is recognized only by a consciousness he does not recognize; the bondsman, through the fear of death, service and formative work, reaches a truer independence than the lord, though not yet freedom.
Premises: the struggle leaves two shapes: "The former is the Master, or Lord, the latter the Bondsman" (PhG ¶189); the lord relates to the thing through the bondsman, who is held by his attachment to life: "it is his chain" (PhG ¶190); "a form of recognition has arisen that is one-sided and unequal" (PhG ¶191); so "It is not an independent, but rather a dependent consciousness that he has achieved" (PhG ¶192); the bondsman "felt the fear of death" and was "melted to its inmost soul" (PhG ¶194); fear is "the beginning of wisdom" but not enough (PhG ¶195), and "Labour, on the other hand, is desire restrained and checked, evanescence delayed and postponed; in other words, labour shapes and fashions the thing" (PhG ¶195).
Conclusion: "The truth of the independent consciousness is accordingly the consciousness of the bondsman" (PhG ¶193); in shaping the thing he becomes aware "of having and being a 'mind of his own'" (PhG ¶196). Without absolute fear, work yields only "stubbornness (Eigensinn), a type of freedom which does not get beyond the attitude of bondage" (PhG ¶196).
Objection: Marx (1844): Hegel knows only abstract mental labor and passes over who owns the product and what work does to the worker, so the reversal is a consolation; the next shape, stoicism, is free "on the throne as well as in fetters" (PhG ¶199), an inner liberation called independence.
Reply (partly Hegel's, partly the literature's): Hegel does not call the bondsman free at ¶196; the next shapes fail (Argument 9), and real mutual recognition comes in spirit and the Philosophy of Right (Arguments 13–15). Marx carries the argument into economic life rather than refuting it. Debt: no test tells formative work from drudgery. Open: Kojève (motor of history), Lukács (labor), Gadamer (formation of consciousness), Pippin and Brandom (one-sided authority); Buck-Morss on Haiti against Pinkard; Beauvoir and Fanon.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 9: Stoicism, scepticism and the unhappy consciousness (PhG ¶¶197–230).
column2:
Aim: a freedom won by withdrawing into thought, whether it ignores the world (stoicism) or dissolves it (scepticism), cannot hold; the self split between a changing self and an unchanging beyond (the unhappy consciousness) is the honest result of both, and the split ends only when the self gives up its private will and finds the universal in its own action, the step to Reason.
Premises: the bondsman's discovery is one of thought: "It is one which thinks or is free self-consciousness" (PhG ¶197); stoicism makes that freedom independent of circumstance: "The essence of this consciousness is to be free, on the throne as well as in fetters" (PhG ¶199); but it has withdrawn from the world, its content "a datum, is given", "merely the notion of freedom, not living freedom itself" (PhG ¶200); "Scepticism is the realisation of that of which Stoicism is merely the notion" (PhG ¶202), yet "Its deeds and its words belie each other continually" (PhG ¶205); so lord and bondsman are "concentrated into one" (PhG ¶206), and knowing itself so, the self is the unhappy consciousness, "a doubled and merely contradictory being" (PhG ¶207); devotion, work and gratitude, and self-mortification fail, until through a mediator it is certain "of having in truth stripped itself of its Ego" (PhG ¶229); that renunciation "is only in one aspect negative" (PhG ¶230).
Conclusion: the self is the unity of particular and universal, and "there has arisen the idea of Reason" (PhG ¶230).
Objection: the transitions are history in disguise: why stoicism, then scepticism, then Christian devotion, unless that is the order of the Roman and medieval world (the liberal critique of Haym, 1857)? Kierkegaard, in spirit: the self that knows its eternal essence and cannot reach it is not a stage to pass through but the existing individual's permanent condition before God.
Reply (the literature's): the claim is that a self taking thought as its whole essence must hold the world off or dissolve it, and either policy splits it; the historical movements are experiments already run, not premises. Pinkard: failures of a community's justification. To Kierkegaard: Hegel agrees the unhappy consciousness cannot be argued out of it; what ends it is shared action, spirit. Open: Wahl's key to Hegel against Pinkard, Pippin and Harris; Left Hegelian critique of Christianity against Houlgate; Butler on ascetic self-formation.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 10: Absolute freedom and the Terror (PhG ¶¶582–595).
column2:
Aim: a freedom that recognizes no will but the universal will of all, and no institution it has not made itself, can produce no law and no lasting work; it can only destroy, and its last object is the individual, so the Terror of 1793–94 follows from the principle, not only from circumstances.
Premises: absolute freedom is the self-consciousness for which "the world is for it absolutely its own will, and this will is universal will" (PhG ¶584), not assent "through a representative" (PhG ¶584); so "all social ranks or classes" are "effaced and annulled" (PhG ¶585); a lasting work would need powers "differentiated into legislative, judicial and executive" and estates (PhG ¶588), but each confines individuals to a part, and the universal will refuses to be represented by a part; any deed by one body means "all other individuals are excluded from the entirety of this deed" (PhG ¶589); so "there is left for it only negative action; it is merely the rage and fury of disappearance and destruction" (PhG ¶589); its "sole and only work and deed" is death, with "no more significance than cleaving a head of cabbage or swallowing a draught of water" (PhG ¶590); "The victorious faction only is called the government", and "Being suspected, therefore, takes the place, or has the significance and effect, of being guilty" (PhG ¶591).
Conclusion: freedom cannot be the bare identity of each will with the universal will; it needs a differentiated order the self can recognize as its own, drawn first as the turn to the "Moral Life of Spirit" (PhG ¶595) and Kant, and in the Philosophy of Right as the state (Argument 15).
Objection: the historian: war, the Vendée and food shortages caused the Terror, so Hegel turns an event into a proof (Soboul). Berlin, Two Concepts of Liberty (1958): positive freedom is the despots' conception, and Hegel's rational state, in which the individual "has his truth" (PhR §258 R), makes the Jacobin claim more durably.
Reply (the literature's): the claim is structural: a revolution whose principle is the bare general will has no criterion to tell opposition from betrayal (cf. Furet). Against Berlin: premise 3 lists what absolute freedom cannot tolerate, separated powers, representation, distinct occupations, which is liberal constitutionalism, and the Philosophy of Right builds on them. Open: Ritter against Habermas on Hegel and the Revolution; Rousseau, Kant or Fichte as target (Comay); Pinkard against Avineri on ¶595.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 11: Being, nothing, becoming (EL §§86–88).
column2:
Aim: the most abstract thought, pure being, cannot be held fixed: thought through, it is indistinguishable from nothing, nothing is the same as being, and the only stable thought of the two is their passing into each other, becoming.
Premises: a science presupposing nothing must begin with the wholly indeterminate: "Pure Being makes the beginning: because it is on one hand pure thought, and on the other immediacy itself, simple and indeterminate" (EL §86); any further determination would stop beginning with being alone; "But this mere Being, as it is mere abstraction, is therefore the absolutely negative: which, in a similarly immediate aspect, is just Nothing" (EL §87); "Nothing, if it be thus immediate and equal to itself, is also conversely the same as Being is" (EL §88); yet they differ, though the difference is "something unutterable, which we merely mean" (EL §88 R); so thought cannot rest in either, and what it has is the passing.
Conclusion: "The truth of Being and of Nothing is accordingly the unity of the two: and this unity is Becoming" (EL §88); "Becoming is the first concrete thought, and therefore the first notion: whereas Being and Nought are empty abstractions" (EL §88 Z). Being and nothing are kept as moments: the first case of Aufhebung. Chalybäus later made this triad the model of thesis, antithesis and synthesis, which Hegel never used as his method (Mueller 1958).
Objection: Trendelenburg (1840, 1843): pure being and pure nothing are at rest, and two motionless abstractions give identity or contradiction, not movement; becoming is borrowed from intuition of things coming to be in space and time, so the presuppositionless start fails. Kierkegaard pressed it: in logic no movement can come about. Analytic: premise 3 equivocates between nothing determinate and nothing at all.
Reply (the literature's, with Hegel's resources): this becoming is not motion; the familiar example only illustrates (EL §88 R). Houlgate: Trendelenburg assumes thought is a fixed content to which movement is added, but an indeterminate thought is not fixed. The equivocation charge needs the category of determinacy not yet earned. Cost: becoming names a logical relation that the rest of the Logic must redeem. Open: ontology (Houlgate, Stern, Beiser) or theory of thought (Pippin, Pinkard, Brandom); Maybee against Forster and Stewart on the triad; Kierkegaard, Houlgate, Inwood on Trendelenburg.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 12: The empty formalism of Kant's moral law (PhR §135; PhG ¶¶419–437).
column2:
Aim: a moral law whose only test is non-contradiction can neither generate duties nor rule out wrongs, since any content not already assumed valid is consistent with itself and its opposite; duties get content from ethical life (Sittlichkeit), and Kant's autonomy survives only inside it.
Premises: on Kant's view, as Hegel takes it, the good will is determined by the form of law alone (PhR §133); duty so understood "is only an abstract universality, and has for its characteristic an identity without content" (PhR §135); its consistency test is "a tautology and indifferent to the content, it accepts one content just as readily as the opposite" (PhG ¶430); "Property per se does not contradict itself", and "community of goods, contradicts itself just as little" (PhG ¶430); "Only if it is really fixed and assumed that private property and human life should exist and be respected, is it a contradiction to commit theft or murder" (PhR §135 R); so "no specific duties can be deduced", and "all manner of wrong and immoral acts may be by such a method justified" (PhR §135 R).
Conclusion: without ethical life Kant's gain "is reduced to empty formalism, and moral science is converted into mere rhetoric about duty for duty's sake" (PhR §135 R); "Where there is nothing, there can be no contradiction" (PhR §135 A). Duties have content in family, civil society and state.
Objection (the Kantians'): the test applies to maxims and seeks a contradiction in willing (Korsgaard, O'Neill); the formula of humanity has content of its own; the Metaphysics of Morals applies the principle to facts of human life, which is not cheating (Wood 1989: the criticism misses its mark). Mill granted the charge for other ends: Kant "fails, almost grotesquely, to show that there would be any contradiction" (Utilitarianism, ch. 1).
Reply (partly Hegel's, partly the literature's): grant maxims, then ask where the maxim's end and the relied-on practices come from: a social world. Pippin: what treating someone as an end requires depends on institutions. Kant did not cheat, but the added content is not shown to follow from autonomy. SEP: part of the force comes from Hegel's definition of morality. Open: Wood against Freyenhagen, Stern and Sedgwick; Kant or Fichte and conscience; Tugendhat against Neuhouser and Wood on criticism within ethical life.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 13: Property as the first embodiment of freedom (PhR §§41–51).
column2:
Aim: property is justified not as a means to needs or a reward for labor but because a free will must have an external existence to be actual, and a thing is the first and simplest; so every person must have property, private property is more rational than common ownership, and how much each owns is, at this level, no concern of right.
Premises: "A person must give to his freedom an external sphere, in order that he may reach the completeness implied in the idea" (PhR §41); what is distinct from the free will is "an object, something not free, impersonal and without rights" (PhR §42); so "Mankind has the absolute right to appropriate all that is a thing" (PhR §44); in possession the will "first became an actual will" (PhR §45), and property "is really the first embodiment of freedom and an independent end" (PhR §45 R); "Since property makes objective my personal individual will, it is rightly described as a private possession" (PhR §46), and Plato's Republic "does a wrong to the person" (PhR §46 R); the will must be shown, so that "The embodiment of my will can then be recognized by others as mine" (PhR §51); "Hence what and how much I possess is from the standpoint of right a matter of indifference" (PhR §49).
Conclusion: "Men are equal, it is true, but only as persons, that is, only with reference to the source of possession. Accordingly every one must have property" (PhR §49 A); "justice demands merely that every one should have property" (PhR §49 A).
Objection: Marx (1843): the entailed estates make the state the property of private property, and the abstract person is the bourgeois owner; in 1844, private property is the product of alienated labor. Waldron (1988): a general-right argument implies a duty to see the propertyless acquire property, so either it does not show each must own, or it condemns a society where many own nothing.
Reply (the literature's, with Hegel's text): Hegel takes the second horn, later in the book: abstract right asks only what a free will requires, and civil society is where Hegel admits the market makes a propertyless class (Argument 14), so the argument is the standard by which that failure is measured (cf. Stillman). Wood and Neuhouser concede the entailed estates. Against Locke: labor is one way of taking possession (§56), not the ground. Open: developmental (Patten, Knowles) or conceptual reading; Ritter against Marx and Losurdo on how liberal; Avineri on the means of production.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 14: Civil society and the rabble (PhR §§182–256, esp. §§241–245).
column2:
Aim: civil society, the market sphere where each pursues his own ends and depends on everyone, is a real and necessary form of freedom distinct from the state; but the dynamic that makes it rich produces a class sunk below its own standard of life and a frame of mind that refuses the society excluding it; civil society cannot cure this by its own means, so it is driven beyond itself.
Premises: in civil society "every one is an end to himself; all others are for him nothing. And yet without coming into relation with others he cannot realize his ends" (PhR §182 A); this right of particularity belongs to "the modern world which alone has permitted every element of the idea to receive its due" (PhR §182 A); unchecked, it "affords a spectacle of excess, misery, and physical and social corruption" (PhR §185); "large fortunes are amassed" while work is divided, bringing "dependence and distress in the artisan class" (PhR §243); when many "sink below the standard of living regarded as essential for the members of society", "a pauper class arises, and wealth accumulates disproportionately in the hands of a few" (PhR §244); "Poverty does not of itself make a pauper", which implies "inner rebellion against the wealthy, against society, and against constituted authority" (PhR §244 A); alms and public works both fail (PhR §245).
Conclusion: "the civic community when excessively wealthy is not rich enough" (PhR §245); "By means of its own dialectic the civic community is driven beyond its own limits" (PhR §246): outward to colonies, upward to the corporation, "a second family" (PhR §252), and the state. (Dyde's "pauper class" renders Pöbel, the rabble.)
Objection: Marx (1843–44): the pauper class becomes the proletariat, a class in radical chains, and a state leaving a class outside the recognition it promises is not the actuality of freedom. Ruda (2011): the rabble's claim is one the system creates and cannot fit. Liberal: colonies export the problem, and corporations protect tradesmen, not day-laborers.
Reply (the literature's, partial): Hegel does not hide the problem: "The important question, how poverty is to be done away with, is one which has disturbed and agitated society, especially in modern times" (PhR §244 A); there are welfare and education duties (§§239–240) and the corporation's honor (§253); Wood and Neuhouser: the framework itself counts this poverty a wrong. SEP (citing Plant): no convincing solution short of changing the economic system. Open: class or disposition (Brooks, Ruda's rabble of the rich); refutation (Marx, Ruda), limit (Avineri) or statable wrong (Wood, Neuhouser, Honneth); market theorist or critic.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 15: "What is rational is actual": the state as ethical life (PhR Preface, §§257–260).
column2:
Aim: philosophy's task is to comprehend the rational structure already present in the institutions of its time, not to design a state as it ought to be; the modern state, distinct from civil society, is rational because it unites subjective freedom with a universal end that individuals know and will as their own.
Premises: "To apprehend what is is the task of philosophy, because what is is reason", and "philosophy also is its time apprehended in thoughts" (PhR Preface); actuality is not mere existence: "existence is in part mere appearance, and only in part actuality" (EL §6 R); so the double saying, in Dyde "What is rational is real; And what is real is rational" (PhR Preface), says reason realizes itself and the truly actual is rational, not that every existing law is justified; the state is not civil society, or "It would then be at one's option to be a member of the state" (PhR §258 R); it is "the realized ethical idea or ethical spirit" (PhR §257), and rationality concretely "is the unity of objective freedom with subjective freedom" (PhR §258 R); "The modern state has enormous strength and depth, in that it allows the principle of subjectivity to complete itself to an independent extreme of personal particularity, and yet at the same time brings it back into the substantive unity" (PhR §260).
Conclusion: the modern state is "the embodiment of concrete freedom" (PhR §260); "To recognize reason as the rose in the cross of the present, and to find delight in it, is a rational insight which implies reconciliation with reality" (PhR Preface).
Objection: it blesses the Prussian state: Haym (1857), and Popper (1945), who made Hegel a father of historicism and totalitarianism, citing "The state is the march of God in the world" (PhR §258 A). Philosophical version: if philosophy only comprehends what is, it loses the standpoint of criticism, and the owl that flies at dusk only records an aged form of life; Hegel's actual institutions include entailed estates, a hereditary monarch and the exclusion of women.
Reply (the literature's): SEP reports a virtual consensus that Popper was wrong: the doctrines favored the Prussian reform era, with trial by jury (Avineri, Knox); the march-of-God line is an Addition from student notes. Actual is evaluative, so it gives a standard; a state may be "defective in various ways" (PhR §258 A) and be criticized by its own concept, as Hegel does on poverty. Applications on estates, monarchy and women fall short of the principle. Open: Stern's neutral reading; Henrich's 1819–20 transcript and censorship (Ilting); liberal (Avineri, Knox, Wood, Ritter) against Haym, Popper, Marx; Pelczynski against Taylor and Beiser.

column1: Reconstruct Argument 16: World history as the progress of the consciousness of freedom (PH Introduction).
column2:
Aim: history is not a heap of events but a rational process, spirit's growing knowledge that it is free, from one free, to some, to all human beings as such; reason achieves this through the passions of individuals who do not intend it, so history's suffering is not meaningless, though not justified case by case.
Premises: philosophy brings to history "the simple conception of Reason; that Reason is the Sovereign of the World" (PH Introduction); spirit's essence is freedom, and history is "the exhibition of Spirit in the process of working out the knowledge of that which it is potentially" (PH Introduction); the Orientals "only know that one is free", so "That one is therefore only a Despot; not a free man" (PH Introduction); Greeks and Romans "knew only that some are free", so "The Greeks, therefore, had slaves" (PH Introduction); "The German nations, under the influence of Christianity, were the first to attain the consciousness, that man, as man, is free" (PH Introduction), a knowledge that must then enter law and institutions; "nothing great in the World has been accomplished without passion" (PH Introduction), and "This may be called the cunning of reason, — that it sets the passions to work for itself" (PH Introduction).
Conclusion: "The History of the world is none other than the progress of the consciousness of Freedom" (PH Introduction). Its meaning is not happiness: "Periods of happiness are blank pages in it" (PH Introduction), and the answer to history as "the slaughter-bench" (PH Introduction) is the growth of freedom, a secular theodicy.
Objection: Popper (1945, 1957): history has no meaning or direction, claims to know its laws are unfalsifiable and license sacrificing individuals; Berlin (1954): instruments of a world-spirit are relieved of responsibility. Second: the scheme is Eurocentric; Hegel says of Africa that "it is no historical part of the World" (PH, Geographical Basis of History), and Bernasconi calls the scheme racially structured.
Reply (the literature's, partial on the second): no predictive law; like the owl of Minerva it looks back, and "peoples and governments never have learned anything from history" (PH Introduction). The claim is a standard: freedom known and institutionalized, justified by genealogy (Pinkard, Pippin). The cunning of reason excuses no one. The structure can be detached and turned against Hegel (Buck-Morss on Haiti); the claims about Africa and Asia cannot be saved. Open: theodicy (Taylor, Beiser) or norms of freedom (Pinkard, Pippin); Bernasconi and Buck-Morss against Stone and Pinkard; Kojève and Fukuyama on the end of history.

column1: Explain the plan of Hegel's system and why it has no foundation in the usual sense (EL §§15, 18; Enc. §§385, 574).
column2:
Plan: philosophy "is subdivided into three parts : I. Logic, the science of the Idea in and for itself. II. The Philosophy of Nature: the science of the Idea in its otherness. III. The Philosophy of Mind : the science of the Idea come back to itself out of that otherness" (EL §18): one structure considered purely, then outside itself in space and time, then returned to itself in minds that know it. Spirit divides again into subjective, objective and absolute spirit (Enc. §385).
Shape: "The whole of philosophy in this way resembles a circle of circles" (EL §15), and at the end philosophy "has gone back to its beginning" (Enc. §574).
Why it matters: there is no first truth on which the rest is stacked; what justifies the beginning is the whole that comes out of it (Argument 1). Idea (Idee) is a technical term for the full rational structure of reality, not a thought in someone's head.

column1: Explain what Hegel means by Geist (spirit) and why the old translation "mind" can mislead (PhG ¶¶25, 177, 438).
column2:
Spirit is reason existing as a shared, self-knowing world. It first appears with recognition, as "Ego that is 'we,' a plurality of Egos, and 'we' that is a single Ego" (PhG ¶177), and "Reason is spirit, when its certainty of being all reality has been raised to the level of truth, and reason is consciously aware of itself as its own world, and of the world as itself" (PhG ¶438). The Preface calls the Absolute as Spirit "the grandest conception of all, and one which is due to modern times and its religion" (PhG ¶25).
Translation: Wallace renders Geist as mind, and so does Baillie in most pages before chapter VI (he switches to spirit there); mind suggests one person's psychology; Hegel's spirit includes will, institutions and history.
Misreading to avoid: not a ghost or a separate cosmic person, whatever one concludes about its metaphysics. Open: a cosmic subject (Taylor, Beiser) or a community's self-correcting practice of giving reasons (Pippin, Pinkard, Brandom).

column1: Distinguish in itself, for itself and in and for itself, and say why the pattern is not a mechanical formula (EL §83; PhR §33).
column2:
An sich: what something is implicitly, as a seed is implicitly a tree. Für sich: what it is explicitly, set over against what it is not. An und für sich: both at once, explicit and at home with itself.
The pattern recurs at every scale: Logic, Nature and Spirit; the Logic's own division into "the notion implicit and in germ", "the being-for-self and show of the notion", and "the notion in and for itself" (EL §83); the will's passage from abstract right through morality to ethical life (PhR §33).
Use: the quickest way to find one's place in any Hegel text. Misreading to avoid: a triadic stamp pressed onto every subject; Hegel himself attacked the formalistic use of Kantian triplicity as a lifeless schema (PhG ¶50).

column1: Explain why the Phenomenology is a ladder and a highway of despair, and what Hegel means by experience and by what happens for us (PhG ¶¶26, 78–88).
column2:
Ladder: the individual "has the right to demand that science shall hold the ladder to help him to get at least as far as this position" (PhG ¶26). Method: each shape of consciousness carries its own standard and is tested against it; when it fails, object and standard change together, and this is experience in Hegel's sense, the "Science of the Experience of Consciousness" (PhG ¶88).
Despair: "the road can be looked on as the path of doubt, or more properly a highway of despair" (PhG ¶78), unlike ordinary doubt, after which "the matter is taken as it was before" (PhG ¶78). The goal is where knowledge "is no longer compelled to go beyond itself" (PhG ¶80): absolute knowing.
For us: the observing philosophers see each transition as a process, while for consciousness the result "has merely the character of object" (PhG ¶87). The order of shapes is logical, not a dated history, though from chapter VI it borrows historical material.

column1: Explain determinate negation and why it lets the Phenomenology claim a necessary sequence without an outside plan (PhG ¶79; EL §§81–82).
column2:
The sceptic "always sees in the result only pure nothingness, and abstracts from the fact that this nothing is determinate, is the nothing of that out of which it comes as a result" (PhG ¶79). A refutation has content: it shows why the position failed, which tells us what a better one must do.
"When once, on the other hand, the result is apprehended, as it truly is, as determinate negation, a new form has thereby immediately arisen" (PhG ¶79).
Why it matters: each new shape is the old one's failure, understood, so the sequence needs no plan imported from outside. Used by the understanding alone, negation is merely negative and "Dialectic becomes Scepticism" (EL §81 R); taken determinately, "The result of Dialectic is positive, because it has a definite content" (EL §82 R). Brandom reads it as the relations of incompatibility that make content determinate.

column1: Explain Aufhebung (sublation) and its three senses (PhG ¶¶2, 113; EL §88).
column2:
Definition: "to supersede (aufheben) is at once to negate and to preserve" (PhG ¶113), and the word also means to lift up. In ordinary German the verb means to cancel, as a law is repealed, and to keep, as a letter is put away; Hegel uses all three senses at once. What is sublated no longer stands as a self-sufficient truth, survives as a moment of something larger, and is raised to a higher level.
Image: the bud "disappears when the blossom breaks through, and we might say that the former is refuted by the latter" (PhG ¶2), yet the stages are moments of one organic unity, each as necessary as the other.
First case in the Logic: being and nothing are kept in becoming as its moments (EL §88). Translations: modern English "sublate"; Baillie "supersede" or "cancel".

column1: Explain Anerkennung (recognition) and why Hegel makes it constitutive of selfhood (PhG ¶¶175–184).
column2:
Desire defeats itself, and "Self-consciousness attains its satisfaction only in another self-consciousness" (PhG ¶175). A self-consciousness exists "by the fact that it exists for another self-consciousness; that is to say, it is only by being acknowledged or 'recognised'" (PhG ¶178).
In its concept recognition is reciprocal: "They recognise themselves as mutually recognising one another" (PhG ¶184), since a recognition extracted from someone I do not recognize in turn is worth nothing to me. Its first appearance, though, is a life-and-death struggle (Argument 7).
Background: Fichte's summons and the Jena writings (SEP, 'Recognition'). Misreading to avoid: not a courtesy added to an already complete self. Open: Honneth's love, law and esteem; Brandom's recognition as the source of normative authority; Kojève's desire for another's desire.

column1: Explain the reversal in lordship and bondage and why the rendering master and slave can mislead (PhG ¶¶189–196).
column2:
The struggle ends when one party prefers life and yields, becoming bondsman to the other's lord. The lord is recognized only by someone he does not recognize, so "The truth of the independent consciousness is accordingly the consciousness of the bondsman" (PhG ¶193). The bondsman has felt absolute fear, and "albeit the fear of his lord is the beginning of wisdom" (PhG ¶195), fear is not enough; "Through work and labour, however, this consciousness of the bondsman comes to itself" (PhG ¶195), because in the formed thing his activity lasts.
Translation: Herrschaft und Knechtschaft, Baillie's Lordship and Bondage; Knecht covers servant and serf, and slave became standard through Kojève's French.
Misreading to avoid: not a literal theory of historical slavery, and the bondsman is not yet free (stoicism follows). Uses: Kojève, Marx, Beauvoir, Fanon.

column1: Explain the unhappy consciousness and how it grows out of stoicism and scepticism (PhG ¶¶197–230).
column2:
Stoicism is free "on the throne as well as in fetters" (PhG ¶199) by withdrawing from a world it cannot change; scepticism carries the withdrawal through, dissolving every determinate claim, but lives by the claims it denies.
The unhappy consciousness takes the contradiction into itself: "the consciousness of self as a divided nature, a doubled and merely contradictory being" (PhG ¶207), torn between a changeable self and an unchangeable beyond it can neither reach nor give up; each effort to rise is "a struggle against an enemy, victory over whom really means being worsted" (PhG ¶209).
Exit: renouncing its own will affirms the will as universal, and "there has arisen the idea of Reason" (PhG ¶230).
Note: the medieval Christian reading is Baillie's and later commentators' gloss, not Hegel's label. Open: Wahl (the key to all of Hegel); Kierkegaard (a permanent condition); Butler (ascetic self-formation).

column1: Explain how the Spirit chapter turns shapes of consciousness into forms of social life, from Antigone to self-alienation (PhG VI.A–B, ¶¶437–476).
column2:
From chapter VI the shapes are worlds, not stances of a single knower. Chapter V ends with the ethical consciousness for which laws simply hold, as for Antigone, who "takes them for the unwritten and unerring law of the gods" (PhG ¶437).
The Greek ethical world (VI.A), read through Sophocles' Antigone, holds the human law of the city and the divine law of the family in immediate harmony; their collision in Creon and Antigone destroys it. Then come the Roman world of legal persons and Entfremdung, alienation, in Baillie "Spirit in self-estrangement" (VI.B): spirit's condition in a world it has made but experiences as foreign, through culture and the Enlightenment's struggle with faith, to absolute freedom and the Terror (Argument 10).
Misreading to avoid: Hegel's alienation is not yet Marx's economic concept.

column1: Explain the three sides of every logical thought: understanding, dialectic and speculation (EL §§79–82).
column2:
Logical doctrine has three sides: "the Abstract side, or that of understanding", "the Dialectical, or that of negative reason", and "the Speculative, or that of positive reason" (EL §79). The understanding fixes concepts and holds them apart (finite and infinite, one and many); in the dialectical moment "these finite characterisations or formulae supersede themselves, and pass into their opposites" (EL §81); and "The Speculative stage, or stage of Positive Reason, apprehends the unity of terms (propositions) in their opposition" (EL §82).
Two cautions from the text: "These three sides do not make three parts of logic, but are stages or 'moments' in every logical entity" (EL §79); and dialectic is not an art applied from outside but "the life and soul of scientific progress" (EL §81 R).
Misreading to avoid: understanding and reason are not two separate faculties of a mind, and speculative does not mean idle guessing.

column1: Explain why thesis, antithesis, synthesis is not Hegel's method, and where the formula came from (SEP 'Hegel's Dialectics' §1; Mueller 1958).
column2:
The three terms are Fichte's. The SEP article states that Hegel "never adopted Fichte's triadic 'thesis—antithesis—synthesis' language in his descriptions of his own philosophy" (SEP, 'Hegel's Dialectics', §1), though he apparently used it in lectures to describe Kant. Heinrich Moritz Chalybäus's popular lectures (1837) called Being, Nothing and Becoming the first thesis, antithesis and synthesis and a schema for the rest (Mueller 1958), and Mueller claimed Marx took up the phrasing in Berlin. Hegel himself, in the Preface, attacked a lifeless triadic formalism (PhG ¶50).
Caution: being, nothing and becoming do fit the pattern, as a few other transitions do, and versions of the triad reading have defenders (Forster, Stewart); many transitions do not (Maybee).
Practice: look for a position that, taken at its word, contradicts itself, and ask what that failure teaches; the third term is often the first position's own truth, not a compromise.

column1: Explain what Hegel means by Begriff (concept; Wallace's notion) and the Idea, and what logic is for him (EL §§19, 83, 163, 213).
column2:
Logic: "Logic is the science of the pure Idea ; pure, that is, because the Idea is in the abstract medium of Thought" (EL §19). Not formal logic but the study of the thought-determinations through which anything at all is thought, derived from one another without borrowing from experience, in three divisions: Being, Essence, and the Concept (EL §83).
Begriff: a thought that develops its own determinations and unites universality, particularity and individuality (EL §163); not a general idea abstracted from cases.
Idea: "the absolute unity of the notion and objectivity" (EL §213), the full rational structure of reality, not a mental representation. The Logic ends in the absolute Idea, the method at work through all the categories.
Open: are these the structures of being itself (Houlgate, Stern) or of any thinking that could count as knowledge (Pippin)?

column1: Explain what Hegel means by Wirklichkeit (actuality) and how it changes the reading of the double saying (PhR Preface; EL §6 R).
column2:
Dyde's Preface has "What is rational is real; And what is real is rational" (PhR Preface), where real renders wirklich, which the Encyclopaedia's translator gives as actual.
Hegel's own gloss: "existence is in part mere appearance, and only in part actuality" (EL §6 R); the contingent, the erroneous and the evil exist, but do not deserve "the emphatic name of an actual" (EL §6 R). Actuality is existence that embodies its rational structure, the unity of essence and existence in the Logic's Doctrine of Essence.
Why it matters: the saying is not a blessing on whatever exists but a standard, so a state may be "defective in various ways" (PhR §258 A) and be criticized by its own concept. Open: Stern's neutral reading; Henrich's 1819–20 transcript variant and the censorship question (Ilting).

column1: Explain the owl of Minerva and Hegel's claim that philosophy is its own time apprehended in thoughts (PhR Preface).
column2:
Task: "To apprehend what is is the task of philosophy, because what is is reason" (PhR Preface); a philosophy that "builds up a world as it ought to be" lives only in opinion (PhR Preface). "every one is a son of his time; so philosophy also is its time apprehended in thoughts" (PhR Preface), and it can no more leap beyond its world than an individual can "jump over Rhodes" (PhR Preface).
The image: "When philosophy paints its grey in grey, one form of life has become old", and "The owl of Minerva takes its flight only when the shades of night are gathering" (PhR Preface).
Why it matters: philosophy comprehends a form of life once it has matured; it neither prescribes nor predicts, which cuts against both Popper's historicism charge and any end-of-history prophecy. The cost, pressed by critics: it may lose the standpoint of criticism (Argument 15).

column1: Explain Hegel's concept of right and of the will that wills the free will (PhR §§4, 27, 29, 33).
column2:
Freedom and the will: "Thus freedom constitutes the substance and essential character of the will, and the system of right is the kingdom of actualized freedom" (PhR §4), "a second nature" (PhR §4). Right is wider than law: "Right, therefore, is, in general, freedom as idea" (PhR §29).
Freedom is neither the bare ability to abstract from every content (made into a politics, the fury of the Terror) nor the ability to choose whatever one happens to want (which depends on contents one has not chosen). The will is fully free when it wills freedom embodied in a world: "the abstract conception of the idea of the will is in general the free will which wills the free will" (PhR §27).
Plan (PhR §33): abstract right, the will immediate in an external thing; morality, the will turned back into itself; ethical life, the unity of the two.

column1: Explain abstract right and why it is abstract (PhR §§36, 41, 49).
column2:
Abstract right treats persons as bare bearers of rights, abstracting from everything particular about them. Its command: "Be a person and respect others as persons" (PhR §36).
A person "must give to his freedom an external sphere" (PhR §41): property (Argument 13), justified by freedom, not need. Abstract right then runs through contract, in which two wills recognize each other in exchanging property, and wrong, in which a particular will sets itself against right and punishment restores it.
Why abstract: it sets aside wants, talents and circumstances, so "what and how much I possess is from the standpoint of right a matter of indifference" (PhR §49); distribution is a question for civil society.

column1: Distinguish Moralität (morality) from Sittlichkeit (ethical life) and say why Hegel puts ethical life above morality (PhR §§105, 135, 142).
column2:
Morality: "The moral standpoint is the standpoint of the will, not in its abstract or implicit existence, but in its existence for itself" (PhR §105); it "converts person into subject" (PhR §105). Its themes are purpose, intention, welfare, the good and conscience. Kant's autonomy is its achievement, but held alone it "is reduced to empty formalism" (PhR §135 R) (Argument 12).
Ethical life (Dyde: "ethical system"): "The ethical system is the idea of freedom. It is the living good, which has in self-consciousness its knowing and willing, and through the action of self-consciousness its actuality" (PhR §142). Duties are the customs, roles and institutions of family, civil society and state, which people recognize as their own freedom.
Open: does ethical life give up the individual's right to criticize institutions (Tugendhat) or keep it inside them (Neuhouser, Wood)?

column1: Explain Hegel's civil society and how it differs from the state and from the contract theorists' civil society (PhR §§182–189).
column2:
Definition: "The concrete person, who as particular is an end to himself, is a totality of wants and a mixture of necessity and caprice", but "each establishes and satisfies himself by means of others" (PhR §182): "the realm of difference, intermediate between the family and the state" (PhR §182 A). Dyde calls it the "civic community".
Contents: the system of needs, read in the political economists, "Smith, Say, Ricardo" (PhR §189 R); the administration of justice; the police, in the old sense of public authority over welfare; and the corporations.
Contrast: for Hobbes and Locke civil society meant political society; Hegel separates the two and says contract theorists have described only civil society. Its right of particularity is a modern achievement. Misreading to avoid: civil society is not the state.

column1: Explain the rabble (Pöbel) and why Hegel says civil society is not rich enough (PhR §§241–246).
column2:
When many sink below the standard of living regarded as essential and lose "that sense of right, rectitude, and honour which is derived from self-support, a pauper class arises" (PhR §244). Dyde's pauper class renders Pöbel, the rabble.
Disposition: "Poverty does not of itself make a pauper" (PhR §244 A); it implies "inner rebellion against the wealthy, against society, and against constituted authority" (PhR §244 A).
No internal cure: charity breaks the principle of self-support, and public works add goods when there are already too few consumers, hence "the seeming paradox that the civic community when excessively wealthy is not rich enough" (PhR §245); civil society is driven outward to colonies (PhR §§246–248).
Why it matters: Hegel states a structural problem and leaves it open; Marx turned the class into the proletariat. Open: class or disposition (Brooks; Ruda's rabble of the rich).

column1: Explain what Hegel means by the state and why it is not an arrangement for protecting property (PhR §§257–260).
column2:
The state is "the realized ethical idea or ethical spirit" (PhR §257), "absolutely rational" (PhR §258). If its end were only the security of property and personal freedom, "It would then be at one's option to be a member of the state" (PhR §258 R): Hegel's objection to the contract theories.
"The state is the embodiment of concrete freedom. In this concrete freedom, personal individuality and its particular interests, as found in the family and civic community, have their complete development" (PhR §260). Its institutions: a constitutional monarchy, an estates assembly and a professional civil service.
Misreading to avoid: "The state is the march of God in the world" (PhR §258 A) comes from an Addition compiled from student notes, not Hegel's printed text. Open: liberal (Avineri, Knox, Wood) or an apology for restoration (Haym, Popper).

column1: Explain the cunning of reason and the role of passion and world-historical individuals in history (PH Introduction).
column2:
Passion: "nothing great in the World has been accomplished without passion" (PH Introduction); the Idea and the passions are "the warp" and "the woof of the vast arras-web of Universal History" (PH Introduction). World-historical individuals, Caesar the standard case, pursue their own ends and carry out a larger one they do not know as such.
Cunning: "This may be called the cunning of reason, — that it sets the passions to work for itself, while that which develops its existence through such impulsion pays the penalty, and suffers loss" (PH Introduction). The cost is not hidden: history as "the slaughter-bench at which the happiness of peoples, the wisdom of States, and the virtue of individuals have been victimised" (PH Introduction).
Background: Smith's invisible hand; Kant's unsocial sociability. Misreading to avoid: it excuses no one, since private aims count for nothing in the result. Objection: Berlin, that it relieves agents of responsibility.

column1: Explain absolute spirit and how art, religion and philosophy share one content in three forms (Enc. §§553–577).
column2:
Absolute spirit is spirit knowing itself, no longer in a social world that never quite matches its concept, but as its own object; subjective and objective spirit are the road to it (Enc. §553).
Art knows the absolute in sensuous form (symbolic, classical, romantic; Greek sculpture the perfect fit); the end-of-art thesis says art no longer carries the highest truth for the modern world, not that art will stop being made (SEP). Religion knows it in representation (Vorstellung, Baillie's "picture-thoughts"); Christianity is revealed because its content is absolute spirit (Enc. §564). Philosophy knows it in the concept: "This science is the unity of Art and Religion" (Enc. §572), and the Encyclopaedia returns to the Logic (Enc. §574).
Open: is philosophy the truth of religion or its quiet replacement? The school split into left, center and right after Strauss's Life of Jesus (1835–36) (SEP).

column1: Explain the end-of-history question and why Hegel's own text cuts against an end-of-history prophecy (PH Introduction; PhR Preface).
column2:
The question: if world history is the progress of the consciousness of freedom, and "we know that all men absolutely (man as man) are free" (PH Introduction), has history in principle ended?
Hegel's text: he calls Europe "absolutely the end of History, Asia the beginning" (PH Introduction), but in a geographical sense, and calls America "the land of the future" (PH Introduction) while declining to prophesy about it, since philosophy deals with what is. The owl of Minerva says the same: philosophy cannot say what comes next.
The thesis made famous: Kojève's 1930s Paris lectures, which shaped Hyppolite, Sartre and Lacan; Fukuyama's The End of History and the Last Man (1992) took it into politics.
The usual reply: the principle of freedom for all has been reached, not that history has stopped. Whether Hegel held anything like Kojève's thesis is disputed.

column1: Set out the metaphysical and post-Kantian (non-metaphysical) readings of Hegel as a live debate (SEP 'Hegel' §§2.2–2.4).
column2:
Traditional metaphysical: a metaphysico-religious account of God as absolute spirit known through pure thought; Beiser (and Horstmann) defend a version, and Taylor reads spirit as a cosmic subject.
Post-Kantian: from the late 1980s Pippin and Pinkard, and in more analytic form Brandom and McDowell, read Hegel as completing Kant's critique of metaphysics by socializing and historicizing rational self-determination.
Revised metaphysical: accepts Kant's critique of dogmatic metaphysics but holds that the logic describes the structures of being itself (Houlgate, Stern; also Westphal, Kreines).
The label: SEP reports that "non-metaphysical" was dropped because it suggested Hegel had no metaphysics at all; Pippin now calls the logic a metaphysics "in a new sense".
Test cases: substance as subject (Argument 2), the Logic's beginning (Argument 11), the rationality of the state (Argument 15).
